question: Which of the following is NOT an exception to the 'Law of Demand'?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Substitute goods**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Law of Demand**, popularized by **Alfred Marshall** in **1890**, states that there is an **inverse relationship** between the **price** of a good and its **quantity demanded**, assuming all other factors remain constant.
 
• **Giffen goods** are a unique category of **inferior goods** (such as **staple foods** like **bread** or **potatoes**) where the **income effect** is stronger than the **substitution effect**. When the **price** of a Giffen good **rises**, consumers, being too poor to afford expensive substitutes, actually buy more of the staple good. ***Hence, statement A is an exception to the law.***
 
• **Conspicuous goods**, also known as **Veblen goods** named after **Thorstein Veblen**, are **luxury items** like **designer watches**, **luxury cars**, or **diamonds**. These goods are purchased for **status** or **snob appeal**; as their **price increases**, they become more **exclusive** and **desirable**, leading to higher **demand**. ***Hence, statement B is an exception to the law.***
 
• **Speculative goods** involve assets where buyers **anticipate** future **price movements**. In **stock markets** or **real estate**, if the **price** of an asset **rises**, investors often buy more of it expecting the **price** to rise further in the **future** to secure a **profit**. ***Hence, statement C is an exception to the law.***
 
• **Substitute goods** are products that can replace each other, such as **Tea and Coffee** or **Pepsi and Coca-Cola**. While the **price** of one substitute affects the **demand** for another (**positive cross-price elasticity**), each good individually follows the standard **Law of Demand**; if the **price** of **Tea** rises, the **quantity demanded** for **Tea** itself will **fall**. ***Hence, statement D is NOT an exception to the law.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Cross-Price Elasticity**: This measures the **responsiveness** of the **quantity demanded** for one good to a **change in the price** of another good. For **substitute goods**, this value is **positive**, meaning an **increase** in the **price** of **Coffee** leads to an **increase** in the **demand** for **Tea**.
 
• **Veblen Effect**: First identified in the **1899** book **"The Theory of the Leisure Class"**, it describes **conspicuous consumption** where **utility** is derived from the **exhibit of wealth** rather than the **functional use** of the product.
 
• **Giffen Paradox**: Observed by **Sir Robert Giffen** during the **19th century** in **Ireland**, he noticed that a rise in the **price** of **potatoes** caused the **poor** to consume more of them because they had to cut back on **expensive meat** to afford the **basic staple**.
 
• **Complementary Goods**: These are goods used together, such as **Cars and Petrol** or **Printers and Ink Cartridges**. Unlike substitutes, they have a **negative cross-price elasticity**; if the **price** of **petrol** rises, the **demand** for **cars** typically **decreases**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Demand Curve Shape**: While a **normal demand curve** slopes **downward from left to right**, the demand curve for **exceptions** like **Giffen** or **Veblen goods** slopes **upward**, indicating a **direct relationship** between **price** and **quantity**.
 
• **Consumer Ignorance**: Sometimes, **consumers** judge the **quality** of a product by its **price**. They may buy more of a **high-priced product** assuming it is of **superior quality**, which acts as another **psychological exception** to the law.
 
• **Emergency Situations**: During times of **war**, **famine**, or **pandemics**, people tend to **hoard goods** even when **prices** are **skyrocketing** due to **fear of shortage**, bypassing the traditional **Law of Demand**.
 
• **Necessary Goods**: For **life-saving medicines** or **salt**, the **quantity demanded** remains relatively **stable** regardless of **price changes**, showing **low price elasticity**.
</ul
